crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research
children.blurb: Retrieval-grounded legal research is the practice of having a language model answer legal questions only from documents that have first been fetched and placed in front of it, rather than from whatever the model absorbed during training.

children.name: Adversarial Statutory Interpretation
children.blurb: Adversarial statutory interpretation is the practice of reading a statute from the position of the opposing party, testing how its text, structure and purpose could be turned against the reading a client prefers.

children.name: Brief Drafting with Machine Assistance
children.blurb: Brief drafting with machine assistance covers the use of AI tools to produce, structure, and revise legal briefs, memoranda, and motions.

children.name: Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking
children.blurb: Citation auditing and good law checking is the practice of verifying that every authority cited in a brief or memo still says what it is claimed to say and has not been overruled, superseded, or quietly narrowed.

children.name: Jurisdictional Anomalies and Local Codes
children.blurb: Jurisdictional anomalies and local codes covers the situations where AI law in one place does not match the law next door, or where a local rule exists with no clear counterpart at state or federal level.

sections.body: Legal research and case strategy is the work of finding the law that governs a question, reading it against the facts, and building an argument that survives challenge. Artificial intelligence now enters this work mainly as a retrieval and drafting layer. Systems search case law, statutes and secondary sources, return passages with citations, and assemble first drafts of memos and briefs. The model does not decide what the law is. It surfaces material and proposes language, and a lawyer checks both. The useful shift is speed in the search and assembly stages, not judgment about what the result means.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Retrieval grounded in a real corpus works reasonably well when the corpus is current and the query is precise. Citation auditing is the strongest use, because a machine can compare a cited passage against the source and flag mismatches, though it still misses some and invents others. Adversarial reading of statutes is harder, since it depends on canons, precedent and purpose that resist pattern matching. Drafting assistance produces fluent text that can be confidently wrong on jurisdiction specific detail. The honest limits are these: no system knows whether a case is still good law without a reliable citator, none can be trusted to state a holding without verification, and none carries responsibility for the filing. Output is a lead, not an authority.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from finding law to testing it to writing it up. Retrieval-Grounded Legal Research is the entry point, covering how a system locates authority and why grounding matters more than fluency. Adversarial Statutory Interpretation takes the found text and reads it against itself, looking for the reading an opponent will press. Brief Drafting with Machine Assistance turns analysis into argument and structure, with the caveats that come with generated prose. Citation Auditing and Good Law Checking is the verification step, where every reference is traced back to its source and checked for continuing validity. Jurisdictional Anomalies and Local Codes handles the material that general models handle worst, the local rule, the odd ordinance, the court specific requirement. A reader would start with retrieval to understand the inputs, use interpretation and drafting for the argument itself, and treat auditing and the local anomalies page as the checks that decide whether any of it can be filed.
